analysis.one_liner: Raises the Affordable Care Act's full-time threshold from 30 to 40 hours, shrinking employer coverage duties.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Ways and Means Committee and died at the end of the 115th Congress despite 83 cosponsors, including 6 Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Affordable Care Act, large employers must offer health coverage to employees working 30 or more hours a week or pay a penalty. This bill would have redefined a full-time employee as someone working 40 hours a week for that rule, so employers would no longer owe coverage or penalties for the millions of workers scheduled between 30 and 39 hours. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and received no further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Large employers — especially in retail, restaurants, hospitality, and staffing, where 30-to-39-hour schedules are common — would avoid both the coverage requirement and the penalties for workers in that range. Some workers whose hours were capped below 30 might see employers raise them toward 40 without triggering the mandate.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large retail, restaurant, and staffing employers

how_it_helps.text: Redefines a full-time employee, for the employer-mandate penalty, as someone working at least 40 hours a week instead of 30, removing employers' coverage obligation and penalty exposure for workers scheduled 30 to 39 hours.

Counters a known side effect of the 30-hour rule: because employers owe coverage or penalties starting at 30 hours, some employers hold workers just under that line; a 40-hour line moves the point where hours get capped.

analysis.who_pays: Workers scheduled between 30 and 39 hours could lose their employer's offer of health coverage; some who lose it would shift onto ACA marketplace plans, with costs partly picked up by federal subsidies, i.e., taxpayers. People who keep employer coverage are not affected, and employers save the penalty they would otherwise owe.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers scheduled 30 to 39 hours a week

drawbacks.text: The core trade: the bill reduces employer health coverage obligations. Workers putting in 30 to 39 hours a week would no longer count as full-time, so their employers would owe them neither coverage nor a penalty, and CBO scoring of the identical 2015 bill found roughly a million people losing employer coverage and a larger federal deficit as subsidized marketplace enrollment rose.

It weakens the employer mandate for exactly the large, low-wage industries where 30-to-39-hour scheduling is most common, while the employers' tax savings are not tied to any commitment to raise workers' hours or pay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The honest case for the bill is real: a 30-hour line gives employers a reason to keep workers just under it, and moving the line to 40 could let some people work more hours. But the bill's direct effect is to remove the employer coverage obligation for a large band of workers, and the costs — lost coverage offers, more subsidized marketplace enrollment, a bigger deficit — land on those workers and taxpayers. The bill offered nothing for the people who would lose coverage, such as a replacement offer or protection against hour-cutting below 40.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Jackie Walorski introduced the bill on September 14, 2017, with a bipartisan group of original cosponsors including Democrats Daniel Lipinski, Collin Peterson, Kurt Schrader, and Kyrsten Sinema.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax law.
No further action was ever recorded: no markup, no floor vote, and no Senate companion action before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary workers scheduling 30 to 39 hours a week kept the existing rule requiring large employers to offer them coverage; employers avoided nothing because the bill never became law.

for.name: Rep. Jackie Walorski
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled a bipartisan group of original cosponsors.

for.name: Reps. Daniel Lipinski, Collin Peterson, Kurt Schrader, and Kyrsten Sinema
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Kevin Brady, R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill at introduction and never scheduled a markup or any further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was heavily Republican (77 of 83), but the bill was genuinely bipartisan at introduction, with six Democratic cosponsors including several moderate Democrats; no recorded votes occurred.

industries.industry: Large employers in retail, restaurants, hospitality, and staffing
industries.note: These employers concentrate 30-to-39-hour schedules and would have erased both the coverage obligation and the penalties for that band of workers, saving the cost they would otherwise owe. Their gain came directly out of workers' access to employer coverage.
Employer-plan enrollment in the 30-to-39-hour band would shrink, but many displaced workers would move to marketplace plans, shifting revenue to exchange coverage heavily subsidized by taxpayers.

industries.industry: Hourly workers scheduled 30 to 39 hours a week
industries.note: Millions of workers in this band would fall outside the employer-mandate definition, putting their employer coverage offers at risk; any gains from more available hours would be at the employer's discretion.
